q: can I give Motrin to my 8 month old for fever
text:

Do not give ibuprofen if your child is dehydrated, has chickenpox, or has asthma unless a doctor recommends it [2]. Do not alternate ibuprofen and paracetamol unless a doctor or nurse tells you to [2].

Keep breastfeeding or offering plenty of fluids, and watch for signs of dehydration [3].

Get medical advice if:
- You are worried about your child [3]
- The medicine is not helping [3]
- A rash appears with the high temperature [2]
- The temperature lasts 5 days or more [2]
- They are not feeding or not themselves [2]

q: my son threw up twice this morning, what should I give him to drink
text:
Vomiting twice in a morning is often gastroenteritis, which is usually not serious in healthy people but can lead to dehydration, according to MedlinePlus [2]. The main thing is to keep fluids going in.

Wait 20 minutes after a vomit, then give oral rehydration solution — 2 to 5 ml every 5 minutes for an hour, says the SEUP [3]. Watch how well he takes it; if he keeps it down, you can slowly give it more often [3]. Don't use homemade solutions like lemonade or commercial soft drinks [3]. Oral rehydration solutions for children can be bought without a prescription [5].

Get help if:
- He is under 3 months and has vomited two or more feeds [7]
- He vomits a lot, can't keep down solids or liquids, or vomits even without drinking [7]
- The vomit is green, bloody, or looks like coffee grounds [7]
- He is drowsy, limp, very thirsty, has sunken eyes, cries without tears, or urinates little [7]
- Severe belly pain or headache [7]

q: how do I know if my child is getting dehydrated from vomiting
text:
Dehydration happens when the body loses more fluid than it takes in, and vomiting is one of the causes, according to MedlinePlus [1]. The main risk of vomiting is dehydration, so the priority is to keep fluids going in, says the SEUP [3][5].

When your child vomits, wait 20 minutes, then give oral rehydration solution — 2 to 5 ml every 5 minutes for an hour [5]. Watch how well they take it; if they keep it down, you can slowly give it more often [5]. Do not use homemade solutions or fizzy drinks [5]. Oral rehydration fluids from the pharmacy are the most helpful for mild dehydration, and sports drinks without caffeine can help a little, according to the CDC [2][4].

Get help if:
- They are listless or very drowsy [3]
- They vomit many times or refuse all fluids [3]
- Vomit is green, bloody, or looks like coffee grounds [6]
- You think they are severely dehydrated [2]

q: my 5 year old has been coughing all night, what can I do
text:
A cough that keeps a child awake at night is common with colds and other respiratory infections, and in preschool children viral infections are the main cause of wheezing, according to the SEUP [2].

There is no home remedy in these passages for settling a night cough. What the sources describe is what to watch for: a cough that comes in fits, vomiting during or after the fits, and exhaustion afterwards points to whooping cough, according to MedlinePlus [1]. In whooping cough the fits get worse and more frequent, especially at night, and can last up to 10 weeks or more [1].

Get help if:
- The cough comes in fits of many rapid coughs, or ends in a whoop [1]
- They vomit during or after coughing fits [1]
- They are exhausted after coughing fits [1]
- The chest sucks in, the ribs and collarbones show, or they breathe faster than normal [5]
- The lips look blue [5]

Asthma is diagnosed by a doctor, not from a cough alone, and in small children it can be hard to tell apart from repeated respiratory infections, according to MedlinePlus [3].

q: my son has been coughing for a week after a cold
text:

q: he has a cough but no fever and is eating normally
text:
A cough without a fever, with normal eating, is usually nothing to worry about. A high temperature is the body's natural response to fighting infections like coughs and colds, according to the NHS [1].

Keep offering fluids and let him rest. If he does develop a fever, the AEPap advises checking his temperature with a digital thermometer, taking it in the armpit, and starting with physical measures: removing extra clothing, giving liquids, reducing physical activity, and a lukewarm bath if he is comfortable [5]. Paracetamol or ibuprofen can relieve the discomfort that comes with fever, with paracetamol the first choice, according to the PUC Chile [4].

Get help if he:
- has a fever and is under 3 months old [1]
- has a fever with a rash [1]
- has a fever lasting 5 days or more [1]
- does not want to eat or is not his usual self [1]
- is dehydrated — fewer wet nappies, sunken eyes, no tears [1]

q: these spots dont seem to bother her but there are more every morning
text:
Spots that do not bother your child are often a rash that can be treated at home, and nappy rash is common in babies [2]. Nappy rash can show as red or raw patches, or as spots, pimples or blisters on the bottom or nappy area, and the skin may be scaly and dry [2]. Keep the area clean and dry, change nappies often, and use a barrier cream at each change; if the rash is not settling, a pharmacist can advise on treatment [2].

Get help if:
- Your child seems uncomfortable or distressed [2]
- The skin becomes itchy or painful [2]
- The spots spread or change [2]
- Your child develops a fever or seems unwell [2]

If the spots are not in the nappy area, or your child has other symptoms, see your doctor.

q: my 6 year old fell from the bed and hit the back of his head
text:
Most head injuries in children are not serious, and most children recover quickly [3][6]. Your son may have a headache, feel dizzy, be sick, or be sleepy — these are common after a knock [1].

What you can do: let him rest, physically and mentally, for 24 to 48 hours depending on how hard the knock was — no sport and no screens during that time, then a gradual return to normal activity [4]. He can eat and drink as usual, according to his appetite [6]. If he has a headache, you can give paracetamol or ibuprofen at the dose your doctor indicates [6]. He may sleep, but after a more significant knock it is worth waking him every 4 hours [6].

Get help if:
- Intense or worsening headache, or one that does not improve with the usual medicine [4]
- Repeated vomiting [4]
- Confusion, or hard to wake [4]
- Changes in behaviour, trouble speaking or walking [4]
- Blood or clear fluid from the nose or ears [4]

Watch him over the first 24 hours after the knock for signs of seriousness [3].

q: what foods should I start with for a baby who just turned 6 months
text:
At around 6 months, your baby is ready to start solid foods, and at first how much they eat matters less than getting used to the idea of eating [2]. They will still get most of their energy and nutrients from breast milk or first infant formula [2].

Start with small amounts and increase them gradually as your baby grows, and introduce one food at a time so you can spot any allergic reaction, such as a rash, diarrhoea or vomiting [1][3]. Offer a variety of foods, following your family's usual foods, and build up to 2–3 meals a day between 6 and 8 months [2][3][6].

Foods to avoid for now:
- No honey before 12 months — risk of botulism [1]
- No cow's milk before 12 months [1]
- No unpasteurised drinks or foods [1]
- No juice before 12 months [1]
- Avoid choking foods like whole nuts, popcorn and whole grapes [1]

If your baby was born prematurely, ask your health visitor or doctor when to start [2].

q: how much water can a 9 month old drink
text: For a 9-month-old, breast milk or formula stays the main drink, and the extra fluids come with meals and during illness, according to the WHO [1]. Offer water in small amounts with meals rather than large volumes, and keep breastfeeding on demand — the AEP says breast milk remains the main food between 6 and 12 months and should be given on demand without reducing feeds [2]. During illness, increase fluid intake, including how often you breastfeed, and offer soft, favourite foods [1]. If your baby is not breastfed, the AEP recommends follow-on formula after 6 months [2]. There is no fixed amount of water a 9-month-old should drink in these passages; let thirst and feeds guide you, and ask your doctor if you are worried about how much they are drinking.

q: my baby refuses vegetables but eats fruit all day
text: It is common for babies to prefer fruit, and the way to build vegetable acceptance is repeated, varied offering rather than pressure. Introduce the whole range of fruits and vegetables gradually, at any daily meal, and vary how you present them — puréed, mashed or in small pieces [2]. The taste for different flavours, including bitter ones like some vegetables, is formed early, and early exposure to different flavours may reduce the risk of refusing new foods [2]. Offer vegetables alongside fruit at meals, and keep offering even when they are refused. Fruit juice offers no nutritional benefit over whole fruit and can displace other foods, so give whole fruit instead [2]. Continue milk feeds alongside meals, and include iron-containing foods such as dark green vegetables, beans and lentils [1].

q: how often should a newborn poop
text:
It is normal for a newborn's pooping to vary a lot: the rhythm and consistency of stools differ from one baby to another, and it is not essential that a baby poops every day, according to the SEUP [3]. What matters more is whether the stools are soft and the baby is comfortable, since constipation means stools that are too hard, with pain or incomplete emptying [6].

For a baby under 6 months, keep feeding as usual with breast milk or formula [3]. Do not give laxatives or enemas without asking your doctor [3].

In a baby this young, check with your doctor if there is:

- Blood in the stool [3]
- Bad belly pain, or the baby is very floppy and crying a lot [3]
- Vomiting many times, not keeping down food or fluids [3]

Your doctor can also advise on what is normal for your baby's feeding.

q: my 9 month old suddenly wakes up every two hours at night
text:
It is common and normal for a 9-month-old to wake at night: night wakings are a natural phenomenon at least during the first year of life, according to the Junta de Andalucía [4]. A breastfed baby may need to feed between 1 and 5 times a night [4].

What you can do: keep night feeds calm and dim, and settle your baby back to sleep after each waking — if your baby sleeps in your bed you may rest better and not notice some of the feeds, since the baby falls asleep again afterwards [4]. Only you can decide how long your baby sleeps in your room or bed [4].

Do not sleep with your baby on a sofa, and do not leave your baby alone to sleep in an adult bed, a waterbed or a mattress that sinks [4].

If you are extremely tired, or if you or your partner smoke, have drunk alcohol, or have taken drugs or medicines that make you sleep more heavily than usual, bed-sharing is not safe [4].

Get medical help right away if your child has severe coughing, serious trouble breathing, or turns very pale or blue in the face, lips or fingernails [3].

q: my son has asthma and is using albuterol more than usual
text:
Using albuterol more often than usual can be a sign the asthma is not fully controlled, and the SEUP says most flare-ups are mild and can be treated at home with bronchodilators [3]. Give salbutamol with a spacer device (and a mask for small children), never straight into the mouth, because it works less well that way [3][7]. A spacer is a plastic container with a mouthpiece or mask at one end and a hole for the inhaler at the other, and a homemade one from a 500 ml plastic bottle can work as well as a bought one [2]. If there is no clear improvement, go to a health centre [7].

Get help urgently if:
- Very agitated or drowsy, or turning blue or pale [7]
- Breathing getting faster, ribs showing, belly or chest pulling in [7]
- Needing inhalations every two hours or less [7]

Avoid smoke and, during the flare-up, exercise and allergens [3].

q: she is making a strange noise when she breathes but is still smiling
text:
A strange noise when breathing can be a sign of croup, which is an inflammation of the voice box and windpipe, according to MedlinePlus [3]. It often starts like a cold and then causes hoarseness, a barking cough and high-pitched sounds when breathing [3]. Most viral cases are mild and can be treated at home, and symptoms usually get worse at night and last three to five days [3].

Keep her calm and comfortable, and offer fluids often. Croup is more common in children between six months and three years, and in autumn and winter [3].

Get help if:
- Breathing becomes difficult or she seems to be struggling [3]
- She is drowsy, floppy or very irritable [1][4]
- Her ribs pull in or her chest sinks with each breath [1][4]
- She is breathing fast or tiring when walking or running [1]
- Her colour looks wrong [4]

If you are worried about her breathing, call your doctor straight away [3].

q: my 6 year old says his chest hurts when he takes a deep breath
text:
Chest pain when breathing deeply can have several causes, and one of them is asthma: chest tightness that makes it hard to breathe deeply is a common symptom, according to the WHO [1]. Symptoms like this are often worse at night or during exercise, and can also be triggered by a cold, dust, smoke, pollen or strong smells [1]. Because symptoms like these can be caused by other conditions too, the WHO advises talking to a healthcare provider [1].

The SEUP says to watch at home for difficulty breathing — ribs showing or the chest sinking in, fast breathing, or getting tired when walking or running — and for chest pain when breathing [2]. Go to the emergency department if your child's general condition worsens, if they are listless, sleepy or very irritable, or if breathing becomes difficult [2]. Chest pain on breathing is also listed by the SEUP as a reason to be seen urgently, to rule out complications [5].

q: my daughter is crying nonstop after a fall and wont calm down
banner: 🚨 With these symptoms your child should be seen in the emergency department today, without waiting. | Reason: A fall down stairs or from more than a metre, or crying that will not settle after a knock: get a doctor to see them today

Crying that will not settle after a knock is a reason for a doctor to see her today, and the SEUP says a fall from more than a metre or a child under three months should also be checked in the emergency department [4].

While you get her seen, keep her calm and do not leave her alone. The SEUP advises watching a child closely in the first 24 hours after a knock for signs of seriousness [2].

- Intense or worsening headache that does not improve with the usual medicine
- Repeated vomiting
- Disorientation or confusion; in very small children, being irritable or hard to wake

- A wound that is deep, dirty or won't stop bleeding
- Muscle stiffness or spasms, especially of the jaw or neck [5]
- Trouble swallowing or breathing [5]
- Fever with sweating [5]

q: I found a lump behind my baby's ear, should I worry
banner: 🚨 With these symptoms your child should be seen in the emergency department today, without waiting. | Reason: Swelling or redness behind the ear, or the ear pushed forward: it should be seen today
text:
A lump behind the ear in a baby is often a swollen lymph node, which can happen with ear infections or other infections, and ear infections are very common in children [2][6]. Most ear infections clear up on their own within 3 days, though symptoms can sometimes last up to a week [2].

While you wait to be seen, treat any pain: give paracetamol or ibuprofen every 6 to 8 hours for the first 1 to 2 days, before the pain builds up [3]. Do not put anything in the ear to ease the pain, and keep the ear dry, especially if it has been discharging [3]. If your baby is feeding, frequent saline nose washes can help [3]. It is normal for them to have a small appetite, so do not force them to eat [3].

Watch for signs it is getting worse: redness, pain or swelling behind the ear, or the ear pushed forward [5]; a lot of drowsiness or being very irritable [5]; or no improvement after 48 to 72 hours of pain relief [5].

q: my teenager fainted during soccer practice
banner: 🚨 With these symptoms your child should be seen in the emergency department today, without waiting. | Reason: Fainting during exercise, or with palpitations or chest pain: get them seen in the emergency department today
text:
Fainting is a brief, sudden loss of consciousness that happens when not enough blood or oxygen reaches the brain, according to the SEUP [2]. It can be triggered by extreme heat, pain, fear, anxiety, standing still for a long time, or standing up too quickly [2].

While they recover: if they feel unwell again, have them sit or lie down right away, breathe slowly and deeply [6]. If they lose consciousness, lay them down with their legs raised and their head to one side so they breathe better [6]. Once the discomfort and weakness have passed, they can get up slowly — sitting first, then standing after a few minutes [6]. They usually recover within a couple of minutes after resting [6].

Get help now if:
- They are not breathing or cannot be woken within 1 minute [3]
- They have not fully recovered, or have trouble speaking or moving [3]
- Chest pain or a pounding, fluttering or irregular heartbeat [3]
- They fainted while exercising [3][5]
- They are shaking or jerking [3]

Fainting during exercise is a reason to be checked [5].

q: my child says everything looks blurry after getting hit in the face with a ball
banner: 🚨 With these symptoms your child should be seen in the emergency department today, without waiting. | Reason: Something stuck in the eye, or a blow to the eye: do not rub it or try to remove it; get it seen in the emergency department today
text:
Blurred vision after a blow to the face needs to be checked, and the SEUP says a head injury can cause symptoms like dizziness, confusion, nausea, vomiting and drowsiness [2]. While you get the eye seen today, keep your child still and calm, and do not let them rub the eye or try to remove anything from it [1].

Get help straight away if, according to MedlinePlus, your child has: a headache that gets worse or does not go away [5]; repeated vomiting or nausea [5]; trouble speaking [5]; weakness or numbness in the arms or legs [5]; growing confusion, restlessness or agitation [5].

After a head knock, the SEUP advises rest from physical and mental activity for 24 to 48 hours, with no sport and no screens, then a gradual return to normal activities [6].

q: my son is vomiting and cant keep even small sips down
banner: 🚨 With these symptoms your child should be seen in the emergency department today, without waiting. | Reason: Vomits everything and keeps nothing down: it is a danger sign — get seen today
text:
Vomiting that stops your child keeping fluids down needs to be seen today, and the most important thing while you get there is to keep offering fluids in small amounts [3]. Offer small sips of rehydration solution to replace lost fluids — your pharmacist can recommend one [2]. If your child is breastfed, carry on breastfeeding and try giving small feeds more often than usual [3]. If they are on formula or solid foods, give small sips of water between feeds [3]. Do not make formula weaker, and do not give fruit juice or fizzy drinks, as these can make vomiting worse [2].

Get help now if:
- Vomiting a lot, not keeping down solids or liquids, or vomiting even with nothing in the stomach [6]
- Vomiting that is green, contains blood, or looks like brown coffee grounds [6]
- Drowsy, floppy, very thirsty, sunken eyes, crying without tears, or passing little urine [6]
- Severe tummy pain or headache [6]
- Under 3 months old and has vomited two or more feeds [6]

q: my child fell from a second story window but seems okay
banner: 🚨 With these symptoms your child should be seen in the emergency department today, without waiting. | Reason: A fall down stairs or from more than a metre, or crying that will not settle after a knock: get a doctor to see them today
text:
A knock on the head is a common injury, and the skull is hard and protects the brain, according to MedlinePlus [4]. After a head injury, the SEUP advises physical and mental rest for 24 to 48 hours, depending on how hard the blow was — no sport and no screens during that time, then a gradual return to normal activity [5].

Get help immediately if there is a headache that worsens or does not improve, repeated vomiting, seizures, trouble waking, dilated pupils, difficulty speaking, weakness or numbness in the arms or legs, poor coordination, or growing confusion or agitation [4]. Also watch for intense or worsening headache, repeated vomiting, disorientation or confusion, irritability or difficulty waking in a very young child, behaviour changes, trouble walking or speaking, or blood or clear fluid from the nose or ears [5].

text: A swallowed button battery is a medical emergency: it can burn the oesophagus within hours, so the child needs to be seen straight away [6]. q: mi niño tiene asma y le cuesta un poquito respirar
banner: 🚨 Llama ahora al 911 o acude a urgencias. | Motivo: Dificultad para respirar grave (se marcan las costillas, respira muy rápido, pausas en la respiración, color azulado)
text:
El asma puede causar episodios de tos, dificultad para respirar y silbidos en el pecho por obstrucción de los bronquios, según la SEUP [2]. En casa, administra de 2 a 4 pulsaciones de salbutamol, de una en una, con cámara espaciadora (y mascarilla facial si es pequeño), y repite esa dosis a los 10-15 minutos [6]. Mantenlo en reposo, sin ejercicio, y evita el humo del tabaco o la contaminación [6]. Si toma tratamiento de mantenimiento, debe seguir con él durante la crisis [6].

Busca ayuda si:
- Está muy agitado o somnoliento, o se pone morado o pálido [3].
- Le cuesta más respirar: respira cada vez más deprisa, se le marcan las costillas o se le hunde el pecho [3].
- Necesita inhalaciones cada dos horas o menos [3].
- Tiene los labios morados o está cada vez más decaído, con dificultad para hablar o comer [7].

Si la crisis no cede con el tratamiento en casa, acude lo antes posible a un centro sanitario y lleva la cámara espaciadora [6].
